summary: German has eight subject pronouns – ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie – plus the polite Sie. A subject pronoun is never left out, because the verb ending alone is not enough (Ich bin …, not *Bin …). er, sie and es follow the grammatical gender of the noun, not the real sex: der Tisch → er, die Lampe → sie, das Mädchen → es. Three words look alike: sie (she, verb in -t), sie (they, verb in -en) and Sie (you, polite, capital S, verb in -en).

askYourself: Who is the subject: me (ich), the person I talk to, or someone/something else?
Am I talking to one person or several – and do I say du or Sie to them?
Is it a thing? Then what is the gender of its noun: der → er, die → sie, das → es?
One or several? Several people or things are always sie, with the verb in -en (sie sind).
Polite Sie: did I write the capital S and use the “they” form of the verb?
steps: Choose the pronoun by person, number, gender of the noun and du/Sie.
Give the verb the matching ending.

traps: Never drop the pronoun: Ich bin müde, not *Bin müde – the verb ending alone is not enough.
ich is written with a small letter inside a sentence; only the polite Sie (and Ihnen, Ihr) takes a capital.
A girl is es in grammar (das Mädchen … es), though people often say sie once they know her name.
Sie (polite) takes the verb of “they”: Sie sind, never *Sie bist / *Sie ist.
ihr (you, plural) is also ihr = (to) her and ihr = her/their (possessive); the verb shows which: ihr seid.

quiz.why: der-nouns are er, even for things.
Every plural is sie, whatever the gender.

quiz.q: You talk to your new boss. “You” is …
You talk to two friends at once. “You” is …
quiz.why: Several people you each say du to: ihr.

quiz.q: Which form goes with polite Sie?
quiz.why: Sie takes the verb form of “they”.

seeAlso.note: Arabic splits “you” and “they” by gender (anta / anti, hum / hunna) and has a dual (antumā, humā); the pronoun is often dropped because the verb shows the person.
Hebrew also splits “you” and “they” by gender (atá / at, atem / aten, hem / hen); in the past tense ani / ata can be left out, in the present not.
Chinese has one spoken tā for he / she / it (他 / 她 / 它 differ only in writing), plural with 们 (我们, 你们, 他们) and a polite 您 – no endings, no cases.
The pronoun chooses the form of sein: ich bin, du bist, er ist …

notes.text: Greek can drop the pronoun (είμαι κουρασμένος); German never can: Ich bin müde. αυτός / αυτή / αυτό follow the noun’s gender like er / sie / es, but polite εσείς takes the 2nd plural, while Sie takes the form of “they” (Sie sind).

он / она / оно follow the grammatical gender of the noun exactly like er / sie / es (стол → он, der Tisch → er). The polite вы is the 2nd plural; German Sie is the 3rd plural with a capital S, and ihr is a separate plural “you”.

Spanish leaves the pronoun out (Soy profesor); German must say Ich bin Lehrer. There is no everyday subject pronoun for things in Spanish (Es grande); German says Er / Sie / Es ist groß by the noun’s gender. usted takes the 3rd singular, but Sie always takes the plural form: Sie sind.
it covers every thing in English; German uses er, sie or es by the noun’s gender: der Tisch → er, die Lampe → sie. you is one word for du, ihr and Sie. ich is lower-case inside a sentence, unlike I.

Obligatory pronouns and il / elle for things by gender (la table → elle) work as in German, but German adds a neuter es. vous is polite and plural at once; German splits it into Sie (polite) and ihr (several friends).

vah / vo is he, she and it; the gender shows only on the verb (vah jātā hai / vah jātī hai). German shows it in the pronoun (er / sie / es) and never on the verb. Hindi has three degrees of “you” (tū, tum, āp), German two (du, Sie) plus the plural ihr.

u is he and she, and the pronoun is often left out because the verb ending shows the person (miravam). German has er / sie / es and needs the pronoun every time. šomā is polite like Sie, but it is the 2nd plural, Sie the 3rd.
to / tī / te (he, she, it) have three genders like er / sie / es. German wir has no inclusive / exclusive split: it is used for āpaṇ and āmhī alike.

Arabic marks gender in “you” (anta / anti) and has dual pronouns; German du has no gender and there is no dual. huwa / hiya for things follow the noun’s gender, as er / sie / es do, and there is a third, neuter es. The pronoun cannot be left out in German, even though the verb shows the person.

Hebrew distinguishes atá / at (you, m. / f.) and can drop the pronoun in the past (halachti); German du has no gender and the pronoun is always there. hu / hi for things follow the noun’s gender, as er / sie / es do. Hebrew has no polite pronoun; German Sie is obligatory with strangers.

Turkish drops the pronoun (geliyorum) and o is he, she and it; German must say ich komme and choose er / sie / es by the noun’s gender. siz is polite and plural; German has Sie for polite and ihr for several friends.

Japanese often leaves the person out and avoids “you” (anata), using names or titles instead. In German every clause needs its subject pronoun, and du / Sie is a grammatical choice made with every sentence.
Korean often omits pronouns and shows respect in the verb ending. German needs a pronoun in every clause, and respect is the pronoun Sie with the verb form of “they”.
hän is he and she, and minä / sinä can be dropped (olen opettaja); German says Ich bin Lehrer and chooses er / sie / es by the noun’s gender – even for things, where Finnish says se.
ő is he and she, and the pronoun is usually dropped (vagyok); German needs it. The polite ön / maga takes a 3rd-person verb – like German Sie, which also takes a 3rd-person (plural) form: Sie sind.
The subject is a prefix on the verb (ninasoma, anasoma), and yeye means he and she. German uses separate pronouns with gender (er / sie / es) and needs them in every clause.
The subject is a prefix on the verb, and there is no gender in the pronouns. German needs a separate pronoun in every clause and chooses er / sie / es by the noun’s gender.

他 / 她 / 它 sound the same (tā) and differ only in writing; German er / sie / es sound different and follow the noun’s grammatical gender (der Tisch → er). 您 corresponds to Sie, but German cannot leave the subject out when it is clear from the context.

Vietnamese chooses “I” and “you” among kinship words by age and relation (anh, chị, em, bác …). German has a fixed set: ich, du, Sie, and the choice of du or Sie depends on closeness and formality, not on age alone.

The person of the subject is an ending of the verb, and separate pronouns are used mainly for emphasis; there is no gender. German needs a separate pronoun in every clause and gives things er, sie or es by the noun’s gender.
